This vignette describes the SIGA procedure as implemented in the package, how
its parameters map to the notation of the SIGA paper (Zhao et al.), and where
the package differs from the original code.

## 1. Setting

Consider a two-arm randomised trial with treatment indicator $Z$ (1 =
experimental, 0 = control), an outcome $Y$ and $p$ baseline predictors
$X_1, \dots, X_p$. A subgroup $G$ is defined by conditions on some predictors,
for example $\{X_4 > 1\} \cap \{X_5 = 1\}$. $G$ is *predictive* if the
treatment effect in $G$ is larger than in its complement $\bar G$, and the
predictors in its definition are *predictive biomarkers*. SIGA searches for the
predictive subgroup with the strongest evidence of an enhanced treatment
effect, while controlling

* **multiplicity**: the risk of reporting a subgroup when no predictive
  subgroup exists, and
* **complexity**: the risk of including noise variables in the subgroup
  definition.

| Endpoint | Outcome in the formula | Model | Treatment effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| time-to-event | `Surv(time, status)` | Cox proportional hazards | hazard ratio (HR) |
| binary | logical, 2-level factor or 0/1 | logistic regression | odds ratio (OR) |
| continuous | numeric | linear regression | mean difference |

The argument `direction` states which direction is beneficial: a *lower*
hazard (default for time-to-event), a *higher* probability of the event level
(default for binary; the event level is `TRUE`, 1 or the second factor level)
or a *higher* mean (default for continuous).

## 2. Candidate prescreening

To focus the search on predictors that may interact with the treatment, every
predictor $X_j$ is tested in the model with $Z$, $X_j$ and $Z X_j$, e.g. for
time-to-event data
$$h(t) = h_0(t) \exp(\alpha_j X_j + \beta_j Z + \gamma_j Z X_j).$$
The predictors are ranked by the likelihood-ratio test of $\gamma_j = 0$
(F test for continuous endpoints) and the top $k$ are kept (`n_candidates`).
The paper recommends $k = \lceil p/2 \rceil$ for $p \le 20$ and $k = 10$
otherwise, the package default. Categorical predictors enter as dummy
variables and ordinal predictors with their level codes. `screen = "rf"`
ranks predictors by the difference of random forest variable importance
between the arms instead, and `screen = "none"` keeps all predictors.
Prescreening is repeated in every resample (section 5).

## 3. Genetic representation of subgroups

A candidate subgroup (an *individual*) is a vector of $k$ real-valued genes
$B_j \in [0, 4]$, one per candidate predictor. The initial population draws the
genes uniformly. A gene is decoded as follows.

| Gene value | Numeric or ordinal $X_j$ | Binary $X_j$ | Categorical $X_j$ with $c$ levels |
|---|---|---|---|
| $B_j \le 2$ | not used | not used | not used |
| $2 < B_j \le 3$ | $X_j \le P_{B_j - 2}(X_j)$ | $X_j$ = first level | $X_j \in C_s$, $s = \lceil (B_j - 2)(2^c - 2)/2 \rceil$ |
| $3 < B_j \le 4$ | $X_j \ge P_{B_j - 3}(X_j)$ | $X_j$ = second level | (same) |

$P_u(X_j)$ is the type-7 sample quantile of $X_j$ at probability $u$, and
$C_1, \dots, C_{2^c - 2}$ are the non-empty proper subsets of the levels,
ordered by size and then lexicographically. Every predictor is therefore used
with probability 1/2. The conditions of the used genes are combined with AND.
Patients with a missing value of a used predictor do not belong to the
subgroup. Categorical predictors may have at most 10 levels.

Predictor types are taken from the data: numeric columns are numeric, ordered
factors ordinal, and factors, logical or character columns binary or
categorical. Use `predictor_types` to override, e.g.
`predictor_types = c(stage = "ordinal")`. A 0/1-coded numeric column is
treated as numeric, which is equivalent to a binary split but is less
efficient; code categorical variables as factors.

## 4. Objective function and genetic operators

**Objective.** With $I$ the indicator of membership of the candidate subgroup,
SIGA fits
$$h(t) = h_0(t) \exp(\alpha I + \beta Z + \gamma Z I)$$
(logistic or linear regression with the same terms for the other endpoints)
and uses the one-sided p-value of the interaction $\gamma$ in the direction of
a larger benefit in the subgroup as the objective to be minimised
(`objective = "interaction"`). A subgroup smaller than $MinS$ (`min_size`,
default 10%) gets the worst value 1. As in the original code, the size of a
subgroup is measured by $2 \min(n_1, n_0)$, the numbers of treated and control
patients in the subgroup. Alternatives are `"subgroup"` (p-value of the
treatment effect in the subgroup, set to 1 when the complement has a smaller
p-value), `"differential"` (difference of the Wald statistics in subgroup and
complement) and user-defined functions (see `?siga_control`).

**Operators.** Every generation applies the operators of the Sheffield Genetic
Algorithm Toolbox (package **gatbxr**):

1. *fitness assignment* by linear ranking with selective pressure 2
   (`ranking`): the best individual has twice the average selection
   probability;
2. *selection* of $GGAP \times m$ parents by stochastic universal sampling
   (`sus`; generation gap `ggap`, default 0.9);
3. *line recombination* of consecutive pairs of selected parents
   (`reclin`): offspring gene $= P_1 + \alpha (P_2 - P_1)$ with one
   $\alpha \sim U(-0.25, 1.25)$ per pair;
4. *mutation* with the breeder genetic algorithm operator (`mutbga`), mutation
   rate $1/k$;
5. *reinsertion*: the offspring replace the worst parents (`reins`), so the
   best individuals always survive (elitism).

The search stops after $MaxG$ generations (`max_gen`, default 50) with
populations of $m$ individuals (`pop_size`, default 50). To avoid premature
convergence, $s$ isolated sub-populations (`n_subpop`, default 5) evolve
independently. The fittest individual over all generations and sub-populations
defines the subgroup; ties are broken by the larger subgroup and then by the
simpler rule.

**Reported rule.** Thresholds are replaced by the boundary values observed in
the subgroup (for example $X \le 60$ instead of the interpolated percentile
62.5), and conditions that do not change the membership are removed. The
membership in the data is unchanged.

## 5. Resampling: multiplicity and complexity control

A genetic algorithm always returns a "fittest" subgroup, even without a true
predictive subgroup. SIGA therefore embeds the search in a resampling scheme:

1. Draw $q$ (`n_resample`, default 10) training subsamples $D_h$ of 63.2% of
   the patients without replacement (`resample_prop`; `resample_method =
   "bernoulli"` draws every patient independently with probability 0.632 as in
   the original code). The remaining 36.8% form the test sets $D_{-h}$.
2. In every $D_h$, prescreen the predictors and run the genetic algorithm with
   `resample_subpop` sub-populations (by default as many as in the final
   search, 5). Evaluate the best subgroup by its treatment effect ratio $r^*_h$
   in $D_{-h}$, and record the predictors it uses.
3. Let $r$ be the effect ratio of the complete data and
   $\bar r^* = \frac{1}{q} \sum_h r^*_h$. SIGA reports **no subgroup** unless
   $$\bar r^* < 1 \quad \text{and} \quad \bar r^* \le (1 - \eta)\, r,$$
   i.e. unless the subgroups found in the training subsamples improve the
   treatment effect in new patients by at least $100\eta\%$ (`eta`).
   Only predictors used by the best subgroups of at least a proportion
   $\theta$ of the resamples are kept (`theta`); without such a predictor,
   SIGA also reports no subgroup.
4. Otherwise the multi-population search is run on the complete data with the
   kept predictors.

**Effect ratios.** $r$ is a ratio for which lower values indicate more benefit:

| Endpoint | Effect ratio $r$ |
|---|---|
| time-to-event | hazard ratio (as in the paper) |
| binary | $1/\mathrm{OR}$, the odds ratio of the non-event |
| continuous | $\exp(-\pi d / \sqrt{3})$, $d$ = mean difference / pooled SD |

For continuous endpoints $d$ is the standardised mean difference (with the
pooled standard deviation of the complete data) and $\pi d / \sqrt 3$ the
corresponding log odds ratio under the logistic approximation, so that $\eta$
has the same interpretation for all endpoints. With $\eta = 0.2$ the
standardised effect must improve by about 0.12 standard deviations. In a test
set $r^*_h$ is set to 1 when the subgroup or its complement is empty, and to
missing when it is not estimable or extreme ($r^*_h > 100$ or $< 0.001$).

**Number of resamples.** The paper recommends $q = 100$; the default
$q = 10$ is that of the original code. With it the package reproduces the
false discovery rates of the simulation study of the paper, on which the
recommended $\eta$ and $\theta$ are based (see the validation chapter of the
user manual). Without a predictive subgroup the held-out ratios $r^*_h$ are on
average 10% to 20% larger than $r$ (a subgroup that looks better than average
in the training part tends to look worse in the complementary test part), so
false discoveries occur when $\bar r^*$ is low by chance. Its variance, and
with it the false discovery rate, decreases with $q$: with $\eta = 0.2$ and
$\theta = 0.5$ the rate in the null models of the paper is about 6% for
$q = 10$ (higher with 300 than with 600 patients) and close to 0 for
$q = 100$, which needs $\eta \approx 0.05$ for a comparable rate. With
$q = 10$ the decision for a given data set can depend on the seed; repeat the
analysis with a few seeds, or use more resamples with a smaller $\eta$, before
relying on a borderline result.

**Search effort per resample.** The paper describes a single sub-population
per resample, whereas the original code ran as many sub-populations as the
final search, which is the default (`resample_subpop = control$n_subpop`).
More search effort per resample finds the predictive biomarkers more
consistently, which increases their selection frequencies and improves the
held-out effects. In model B1 of the paper with 300 patients, for example,
the biomarker $X_4$ was used by 67% of the resampled subgroups with one and by
91% with five sub-populations, and the mean held-out hazard ratio relative to
the overall one fell from 0.68 to 0.55. `resample_subpop = 1` makes the
resampling about five times faster.

**Re-using the resampling.** The decision depends on $\eta$ and $\theta$ only
through $\bar r^*$ and the selection frequencies, so `update(fit, eta, theta)`
re-applies the rule without repeating the resampling. Because the random number
streams of the final search are fixed by the seed, the result equals a new call
of `siga()` with the same seed.

## 6. Recommended settings

| Parameter | Argument | Default | Recommendation (paper) |
|---|---|---|---|
| candidates $k$ | `n_candidates` | $\lceil p/2\rceil$ / 10 | $\lceil p/2\rceil$ if $p \le 20$, else 10 |
| population size $m$ | `siga_control(pop_size)` | 50 | 50 |
| generations $MaxG$ | `siga_control(max_gen)` | 50 | 50 |
| sub-populations $s$ | `siga_control(n_subpop)` | 5 | 5 |
| generation gap | `siga_control(ggap)` | 0.9 | 0.8 to 1 |
| minimum size $MinS$ | `siga_control(min_size)` | 0.1 | 0.1 |
| resamples $q$ | `n_resample` | 10 | 100 (10 in the simulations) |
| sub-populations per resample | `resample_subpop` | `n_subpop` | 1 (5 in the simulations) |
| multiplicity $\eta$ | `eta` | 0.2 (binary: 0.25) | 0.15 weak, 0.2 moderate, 0.25 strict |
| complexity $\theta$ | `theta` | 0.5 | 0.5 weak, 0.7 moderate, 0.9 strict |

In the simulations of the paper (and with the package defaults) $\eta = 0.2$
kept the false subgroup discovery rate around 5% (for binary endpoints it was
8.5% in the validation simulations, also with $\theta = 0.7$, and 5% to 6%
with $\eta = 0.25$, the default for binary endpoints), and $\theta = 0.5$ gave the
best balance between detecting all predictive biomarkers and excluding noise
variables. Large $\theta$ (e.g. 0.9)
tends to keep only one biomarker. The settings can be compared with
`siga_cv()`.

SIGA is an exploratory method: the multiplicity control is not a strong
(family-wise) control, and subgroups should be confirmed in independent data
or a subsequent trial.

## 7. Differences from the original code

The genetic algorithm reproduces the original implementation operator by
operator: with the same objective values and random seed, the best objective
value of every generation is identical (see the validation report). The
following points differ.

* **Bug fixes.** (i) A single continuous predictor used in one direction took
  its threshold from the pooled quantiles of all numeric candidates. (ii) A
  single binary factor produced an empty subgroup (`x == ''`). (iii) A single
  categorical factor stopped the search when several were candidates, and
  factors with exactly three levels could only define single-level subsets.
  (iv) The binary prescreening used the deviance instead of the p-value and
  kept the least predictive predictors. (v) The best-subgroup summary could
  produce vacuous conditions `x >= a | x <= b`. (vi) The last generation was
  ignored when choosing the best individual.
* **Objective scale.** The original code used the two-sided interaction
  p-value, replaced by $1 - p$ for harmful interactions with $p < 0.5$. The
  package uses the one-sided p-value. For beneficial interactions the
  ranking of the subgroups, and hence the search, is the same.
* **Resampling.** As in the original code, every resample runs `n_subpop`
  sub-populations (the paper describes one), but exactly 63.2% of the patients
  are drawn, as described in the paper; the original code drew every patient
  independently with probability 0.632 (`resample_method = "bernoulli"`).
* **Thresholds.** The upper condition is $X \ge P$ (the paper writes $X > P$),
  which matters for ordinal predictors.
* **Simulation program.** The original program used the event time as the
  observed time of censored patients (the event indicator is correct).
  `siga_simulate()` uses $\min(T, C)$ by default; `legacy = TRUE` reproduces
  the original data exactly. The noise covariates $X_{11}$ to $X_{20}$ were
  generated with pairwise correlation 0.5 (`noise_rho`).
